front: Which GYN cancers are driven by HPV, and which is driven by estrogen?
back: HPV: cervical, vaginal, and many vulvar cancers. Estrogen: endometrial cancer.
extra: Ovarian cancer is the genetic one (BRCA, Lynch) and is treated mainly with surgery and chemo, not radiation.

front: Besides HPV infection itself, what raises the risk of cervical cancer?
back: Smoking and immunosuppression (which keep HPV from clearing), more HPV exposure, and above all lack of screening
extra: The HPV vaccine prevents new infections but doesn't clear existing ones, so vaccinated women are still screened. Nearly all cervical cancers start in the transformation zone, where glandular canal cells meet the squamous outer cervix.

front: What single mechanism explains most endometrial cancer risk factors?
back: Unopposed estrogen (estrogen stimulating the lining without progesterone)
extra: Obesity, nulliparity, PCOS, unopposed HRT, and tamoxifen. Endometrial is the most common GYN cancer in the US.

front: What is the classic presentation of endometrial cancer, and why is it usually caught early?
back: Postmenopausal bleeding, which prompts an early workup (transvaginal ultrasound and endometrial biopsy)
extra: An endometrial stripe >4 mm in a postmenopausal woman needs a biopsy.

front: Why is every endometrial cancer tested for mismatch repair (MMR/MSI)?
back: To screen for Lynch syndrome, and because MMR-deficient tumors respond well to immunotherapy
extra: Lynch carries a 30-60% lifetime endometrial cancer risk. A young patient with a family history of colon cancer is the classic case.

front: Why can a cervical cancer that grows sideways cause hydronephrosis?
back: The ureter runs through the parametrium, under the uterine artery about 2 cm lateral to the cervix, so lateral tumor can squeeze it.
extra: "Water under the bridge." Hydronephrosis from tumor makes it stage IIIB.

front: Which part of the vagina drains to the groin nodes?
back: The lower third (like the vulva)
extra: The upper two-thirds drain to the pelvic nodes like the cervix, so lower-third involvement adds the groins to the field.

front: In what order does cervical cancer spread through the lymph nodes?
back: Pelvic nodes (parametrial, obturator, internal and external iliac) first, then common iliac, then para-aortic
extra: Endometrial cancer follows the same path but can also jump straight to the para-aortics along the ovarian vessels.

front: Where does vulvar cancer spread first, and what does a positive pelvic node mean?
back: To the inguinofemoral (groin) nodes. A pelvic node is distant (stage IVB) for the vulva.
extra: Lateral tumors drain to one groin; midline tumors (clitoris, perineum) drain to both. Two pathways to vulvar cancer: HPV-associated (younger women) and HPV-independent from lichen sclerosus (older, p53-mutated, worse prognosis).

front: What is the most common site of recurrence after hysterectomy for endometrial cancer, and how is it treated preventively?
back: The vaginal cuff; it is the target of adjuvant vaginal brachytherapy.
extra: The cuff is the sewn-closed top of the vagina after hysterectomy.

front: Which imaging tests stage cervical cancer locally vs for nodes and distant disease?
back: Pelvic MRI (T2) for local extent; FDG PET/CT for nodes and distant disease
extra: FIGO 2018 lets imaging assign the cervical stage.

front: On cervical MRI, what finding indicates parametrial invasion, and why does it change treatment?
back: A break in the dark (low-signal) cervical stromal ring with tumor extending into the parametrial fat. That is stage IIB, treated with chemoradiation rather than radical hysterectomy.
extra: An intact stromal ring essentially rules out parametrial invasion. Tumor is intermediate gray on T2.

front: In cervical cancer, what PET/CT finding usually extends the radiation field above the pelvis?
back: Para-aortic (or common iliac) nodal uptake, which leads to an extended field up to the renal vessels
extra: A PET-positive pelvic node gets a boost. A 3-month post-treatment PET showing complete response predicts excellent outcomes. PET-positive pelvic nodes also get a boost. KEYNOTE-A18: pembrolizumab with and after chemoRT improved survival in high-risk locally advanced disease.

front: What are the four "shells" that every FIGO GYN staging system follows?
back: I = confined to the organ; II = next door (the adjacent structure); III = pelvic side wall or nodes; IV = bladder/rectal mucosa or distant
extra: Place a finding in a shell first; the substage letter just adds a size or depth cutoff.

front: In any GYN cancer, what does a positive regional lymph node do to the stage?
back: It makes it at least stage III, no matter how small the primary is.
extra: Example: a 3.8 cm cervical tumor with a positive pelvic node is IIIC1, not IB2.

front: Which GYN cancers are staged clinically and which surgically, and why?
back: Cervix and vagina are staged clinically (exam + imaging), because many patients go straight to chemoradiation. Endometrium and vulva are staged surgically, because the defining facts come from the specimen.
extra: For cervix, pathology supersedes imaging and exam when available (FIGO 2018).

front: What size cutoffs divide cervical cancer stage IB1, IB2, and IB3?
back: IB1 ≤2 cm, IB2 >2-4 cm, IB3 >4 cm
extra: These matter because IB3 (and higher) gets chemoradiation rather than surgery.

front: In cervical cancer, what stage is parametrial invasion, and what pushes it to IIIB?
back: Parametrial invasion = IIB. Extension to the pelvic side wall or hydronephrosis = IIIB.
extra: Upper two-thirds of the vagina = IIA; lower third = IIIA.

front: In cervical cancer, what is the difference between IIIC1 and IIIC2?
back: IIIC1 = pelvic nodes; IIIC2 = para-aortic nodes
extra: Suffix r = found on imaging; p = proven on pathology.

front: Does bullous edema of the bladder make a GYN cancer stage IVA?
back: No. Stage IVA requires biopsy-proven bladder or rectal mucosal invasion.

front: In endometrial cancer (FIGO 2009), what separates IA, IB, and II?
back: IA <50% myometrial invasion; IB ≥50%; II = cervical stroma involved
extra: Tumor in the cervical glands alone does not make it stage II. Pelvic MRI estimates myometrial depth and cervical stromal invasion, mainly to guide surgery or stage medically inoperable patients.

front: Which endometrial cancer molecular class has the best prognosis, and which has the worst?
back: Best: POLE-mutated. Worst: p53-abnormal.
extra: The other two are MMR-deficient and no specific profile. FIGO 2023 downstages POLE-mutated and upstages p53-abnormal early tumors.

front: Why does GYN oncology try to choose either surgery or chemoradiation, not both?
back: Surgery followed by chemoradiation adds the toxicity of both without a clear cure benefit over picking the right single approach.
extra: Small confined tumors go to surgery; locally advanced or node-positive disease goes to chemoradiation.

front: What is the standard treatment for locally advanced cervical cancer (IB3-IVA)?
back: Pelvic EBRT (about 45 Gy in 25 fractions) with weekly cisplatin, followed by brachytherapy
extra: The 1999 cisplatin trials showed chemoradiation beats RT alone for survival. No routine hysterectomy afterward. Simulation is often done with full and empty bladder scans because the uterus moves with bladder filling.

front: Why can't brachytherapy be replaced by IMRT or SBRT in cervical cancer?
back: Brachytherapy is what delivers the curative dose to the cervix while sparing the bladder and rectum; leaving it out lowers cure rates.
extra: Bulky or parametrial residual tumor gets interstitial needles added. Brachy is planned on MRI (or CT) with the applicator in place; the common goal is HR-CTV D90 ≥85 Gy EQD2 (EBRT + brachy), with bladder, rectum, and sigmoid D2cc limits (EMBRACE).

front: Within what time should cervical chemoradiation plus brachytherapy be completed, and why?
back: About 8 weeks (56 days), because each extra day lowers local control
extra: Treatment breaks let the tumor repopulate.

front: What are the curative options for early cervical cancer (e.g., IB1-IB2), and how should surgery be done?
back: Radical hysterectomy with node evaluation, done open, or definitive radiation (EBRT + brachy), with similar survival
extra: LACC: minimally invasive radical hysterectomy had worse survival. SHAPE: simple hysterectomy is enough for low-risk tumors.

front: After radical hysterectomy for cervical cancer, which kinds of features make up the Sedlis criteria, and what do they trigger?
back: Combinations of LVSI, depth of stromal invasion, and tumor size (intermediate risk). They trigger adjuvant pelvic RT.
extra: GOG 92: pelvic RT cut recurrence roughly in half. The exact combinations are in the reading's checker.

front: What are the Peters criteria after radical hysterectomy, and what do they trigger?
back: Positive nodes, positive margins, or parametrial invasion. They trigger adjuvant chemoradiation.
extra: GOG 109: adding chemo to pelvic RT improved overall survival.

front: After hysterectomy for stage I-II endometrioid endometrial cancer, how does adjuvant treatment scale with risk?
back: Low risk: observation. Intermediate/high-intermediate risk: vaginal brachytherapy. High risk: pelvic EBRT ± chemo.
extra: Risk rises with deep invasion, grade 3, substantial LVSI, older age, and stage II. POLE-mutated tumors can be observed.

front: What did PORTEC-2 show?
back: For high-intermediate risk endometrial cancer, vaginal brachytherapy controlled the vagina as well as pelvic EBRT, with far less GI toxicity.
extra: PORTEC-1 / GOG 99: pelvic RT cut recurrence (mostly vaginal) without improving survival.

front: What is the adjuvant approach for stage III (node-positive) endometrial cancer?
back: Chemotherapy-led: carboplatin/paclitaxel ± pelvic (± para-aortic) EBRT ± vaginal brachy
extra: PORTEC-3: chemoRT beat RT alone, mainly stage III and serous. Immunotherapy helps advanced disease, especially MMR-deficient.

front: Which vulvar cancers can skip groin node evaluation?
back: Stage IA only (≤2 cm and ≤1 mm invasion), because the nodal risk is under 1%
extra: Everyone else gets groin evaluation, with sentinel node biopsy for unifocal tumors <4 cm and clinically negative groins (GROINSS-V).

front: After vulvar cancer surgery, what findings call for adjuvant groin and pelvic radiation?
back: Two or more positive nodes, extracapsular extension, or a sentinel node metastasis >2 mm
extra: GOG 37: groin/pelvic RT beat pelvic node dissection for survival. Weekly cisplatin is often added.

front: When is vulvar cancer treated with definitive chemoradiation instead of surgery?
back: When surgery would require exenteration or destroy the urethra, anus, or clitoris
extra: GOG 205: chemoRT with weekly cisplatin gave a high complete response rate. Residual disease is biopsied and resected if feasible.

front: How is a superficial stage I vaginal cancer treated?
back: Brachytherapy alone (vaginal cylinder)
extra: Thicker or more advanced tumors borrow from cervix: EBRT ± cisplatin plus a brachy boost, adding the groins for lower-third tumors. Before staging, confirm a true vaginal primary: a tumor touching the cervix is staged as cervical, one touching the vulva as vulvar, and many vaginal lesions are metastases or recurrences.

front: What kind of radiation is used for heavy vaginal bleeding from an incurable cervical cancer?
back: A short palliative course (e.g., 8 Gy × 1-3, 20 Gy in 5, or a twice-daily "quad shot")
extra: Choose by prognosis and goals.

front: What are the common acute side effects of pelvic chemoradiation for GYN cancers?
back: Diarrhea, cystitis, fatigue, and low blood counts (from cisplatin plus marrow dose)
extra: IMRT lowers GI, urinary, and marrow toxicity compared with 3D (TIME-C). Vulvar and groin fields add a skin reaction.

front: What late vaginal side effect follows GYN radiation, and how is it prevented?
back: Vaginal stenosis (narrowing and dryness), prevented with regular dilator use
extra: Other late effects: ovarian failure (consider ovarian transposition in young patients), bowel/bladder injury, fistula, insufficiency fractures, lymphedema.
